name: Trilostane

lead: Trilostane is a synthetic steroid that blocks the enzyme 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, which sits early in the production of cortisol, aldosterone and sex steroids. Today it is best known as the veterinary drug Vetoryl, used to treat Cushing's syndrome in dogs.

In bodybuilding forums it has been described as an alternative way of lowering estrogen and cortisol, with the appearance goal of less water retention and a leaner, harder look. Published human research is old and clinical, covering Cushing's syndrome and breast cancer, and none tests it as a physique aid.

paras: Forum users have described short protocols that pair it with other compounds, usually alongside a cycle of anabolic steroids, aimed at managing estrogen and cortisol. This article does not give doses or schedules. Its route is oral, and it is a prescription-only drug.

Reported human effects include gastrointestinal upset, with serious gastrointestinal bleeding and ulcers, reversible low granulocytes and oral tingling. Trilostane lowers cortisol and aldosterone, so hormone balance can be disrupted. It is prescription-only, and in the US it was withdrawn for human use in 1994.

chain: Claimed: less water retention and a drier look
angle.text: Bodybuilders describing it aim to lower estrogen and cortisol so the physique looks leaner and harder. That use is claimed in forum discussion and is not an approved or studied use.

lead: Trilostane is an oral synthetic steroid that inhibits steroid hormone production by blocking 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3-beta-HSD). It is not an aromatase inhibitor, although it is sometimes discussed alongside them.[1] It is sold for dogs as Vetoryl and similar brands.[1]

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding settings, trilostane has been proposed as a way to reduce cortisol and estrogen activity, with the aim of reducing water retention, giving a drier, more muscular look and protecting lean mass. This is a use described by forum members, not a labeled use.[2][3]

Published work on the drug covers Cushing's disease and related conditions in dogs, historical human use in Cushing's syndrome, and advanced breast cancer, where it was given with hydrocortisone.[4][5][6] No human trial has examined it for body composition or appearance.

paras: Veterinary use: trilostane is used to treat Cushing's syndrome in dogs, with US approval in 2008 under the Vetoryl name and EU approval of Trilocur and Trilorale in May 2024. It is also used off-label for canine alopecia X.[1] Reviews cover its role in canine hyperadrenocorticism and newer applications.[7][8]
Historical human use: it was used for Cushing's syndrome, Conn's syndrome and postmenopausal breast cancer, the last alongside a corticosteroid.[1]

Trilostane inhibits 3-beta-HSD, blocking production of cortisol, aldosterone and sex steroids; its metabolite 17-ketotrilostane is more active and is cleared by the kidneys. It also acts as a noncompetitive antiestrogen at the estrogen receptor.[1] A 2025 review notes that by blocking progesterone synthesis from pregnenolone it also raises brain neurosteroids such as allopregnanolone.[8]

Reported effects in humans include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and gastritis; serious gastrointestinal bleeding and ulcers can occur, as can reversible low granulocytes and transient oral tingling. In dogs it is not used with kidney or liver disease, certain cardiovascular drugs, or in pregnancy and breeding.[1]

Trilostane was withdrawn for human use in the United States in April 1994 and remained available in the UK as Modrenal until it was discontinued there.[1] A 1993 multicentre trial compared it with aminoglutethimide in advanced postmenopausal breast cancer.[6]

T Nation forum posts have described short protocols that pair trilostane with other compounds to address cortisol and estrogen during anabolic cycles, framed as a route to reducing estrogenic water retention.[2][3] The drug is prescription-only and sold for veterinary use, and no human study supports the physique-related claims.

No human trials have examined trilostane for appearance or body composition. Clinical studies include a 1989 trial of trilostane with hydrocortisone in metastatic breast cancer, a 1993 multicentre crossover study versus aminoglutethimide, a 2003 trial in dogs with pituitary-dependent hyperadrenocorticism, and a 2004 trial in canine alopecia X.[5][6][9][10]
